Hemophilia

A prospective controlled dental cohort found shorter time to hemostasis when low-level laser therapy was added to standard care. A separate mouse experiment found faster wound closure and included platelet experiments. These findings concern local or experimental outcomes and do not establish systemic control of hemophilia.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A prospective controlled dental cohort found shorter time to hemostasis when low-level laser therapy was added to standard care. A separate mouse experiment found faster wound closure and included platelet experiments. These findings concern local or experimental outcomes and do not establish systemic control of hemophilia.

Summary of the Evidence

Two publications directly examine PBM in hemophilia-related bleeding or healing. One is a prospective controlled cohort of 60 people undergoing dental extraction. The other is a mouse experiment on skin-wound closure. The mouse paper also includes experiments with human platelet-rich plasma and isolated platelets; those are methods within the same publication, not additional studies. The clinical and animal reports are separate investigations, and no patient trial of systemic hemophilia control was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In the dental cohort, 30 participants received standard care plus low-level laser therapy at the extraction socket and 30 received standard care alone. The mean time to hemostasis was 22.42% shorter in the laser group. Tranexamic-acid packs were replaced in two cases in each group. Three controls required sutures and one required cauterization. Because the study was prospective but not randomized, and because it measured local dental hemostasis, it does not show that PBM corrects the underlying clotting disorder or reduces bleeding elsewhere (Kelkar et al. 2023).

Animal evidence

In hemophilic mice with 3-mm skin punch wounds, wounds closed by day 10 after laser treatment and by day 13 after sham treatment; wounds in non-hemophilic mice closed by day 9. This suggests that local light exposure can affect wound repair in this model, but it is not a test of dental care or systemic bleeding in people (Hoffman and Monroe 2012).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The mouse publication also reported greater clot rigidity and platelet activity in human platelet-rich plasma after illumination. Isolated platelet experiments found increased mitochondrial membrane potential and greater binding of coagulation factors to activated platelets. These laboratory findings help describe possible mechanisms but do not represent a separate clinical study.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The dental study’s abstract and database record do not report the wavelength, dose, or exposure schedule, so its protocol cannot be compared reliably with the mouse work. The mouse wounds received visible red light at 650 nm and 12 J/cm² on three successive days. No head-to-head or dose-finding test established an optimal exposure. Direct illumination of a mouse skin wound also differs from treating a human extraction socket.

Interpretation

The clearest human finding is a shorter local hemostasis time in one controlled cohort. Replication with randomized allocation and standardized bleeding outcomes is needed before making a stronger clinical claim.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for reduced post-extraction hemostasis time in people with hemophilia Very low for systemic hemostasis or disease control
Publications and records2 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The local rating is low because one prospective controlled cohort of 60 people reported faster hemostasis, but the allocation was not randomized and the result has not been independently replicated. Mouse and platelet experiments add biological detail, not proof of patient benefit. A larger randomized dental study would strengthen the local estimate. Systemic bleeding outcomes would need separate clinical trials.
